title: the plate that tells a story
hookLine: a bone, an egg, parsley and horseradish: the Passover plate, and why the answer starts with we

cards: A spring night, a long table, chairs borrowed from the neighbors. In the middle sits a plate with odd little things on it: a roasted bone, an egg, some parsley, horseradish, a brown sweet paste. Nobody's eating them yet.
Then the youngest kid stands up, a little nervous, and asks: why is this night different from all other nights?

teach.b: Seder means order. Passover night follows a set order of steps, read from a little book called the Haggadah, which means the telling.
The story it tells is the Exodus: slaves in Egypt, a stubborn king, ten plagues, and a night of leaving so rushed the bread had no time to rise. That's the matzah.

teach.h: THE STORY LAID OUT AS FOOD.
teach.b: The plate is the story laid out as food. Bitter herbs, often horseradish, for how bitter slavery was. Charoset, a sweet paste often made of apples, nuts and wine, looks like the mortar the slaves used for bricks.
A green vegetable, often parsley, dipped in salt water, like tears. The roasted bone recalls the lamb of the first Passover; the egg, an offering brought on festivals long ago.
You taste the story before anyone explains it. Then comes the surprise. The answer to the child's question doesn't start with once upon a time.
It starts: we were slaves. We. The old rule is that in every generation, each person should see themselves as if they personally walked out of Egypt.
Not a history lesson. A memory you're handed.

how: On the first night of Passover (the first two, for many outside Israel), Jewish families hold a seder, reading the Haggadah around the table: the youngest asks the four questions, the story is told in the first person, and matzah, bitter herbs, charoset and a green vegetable in salt water are eaten as part of the telling.

games.q: what's on the plate — tap the pairs.

s: matzah is flat because the bread had no time to rise
the night of leaving came too fast for the dough.
the seder tells the Exodus as something that happened to other people
the answer starts: we were slaves. each person, as if they came out themselves.

games.q: you're at the seder. the story is ancient. how does the old rule say you should hear it?
o: as if you yourself came out of Egypt.
as a legend with a moral.
games.why: in every generation, a person should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: something bitter from this year. Second breath: something sweet that came anyway.
Third breath: hold the two together, the bitter and the sweet, the way the plate does.

wordCard.voice: Seder. Order: Passover night told step by step, with the story laid out on a plate. Fourth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: order. Passover night follows a set order of steps.

carryVoice: Your line: we were slaves. Not they. We. That one word carries the whole night. Day four.
